9053.verbatim: Criteria Corp's article by Dr Matthew Neale (16 June 2022) on the Sackett re-analysis, led by Professor Paul Sackett of the University of Minnesota. The study aggregated and re-analysed data from hundreds of prior studies, incorporating results from tens of thousands of people working in or applying for over 500 different jobs. Compared with the classic Schmidt and Hunter 1998 meta-analysis, the findings are broadly consistent in which methods rank highest: those that directly assess the knowledge, skills and abilities required to do the job in a structured and consistent manner. The most predictive methods in the new study are listed as structured interviews, job knowledge tests, empirically keyed biodata, work sample tests and cognitive ability tests. Two changes are called out. First, the gap between structured and unstructured interviews is larger than previously assessed: structured interviews have more than double the predictive power of unstructured ones, and nearly a third less bias. Second, on the top five methods the new paper finds validities about 25% lower than those reported in previous research. Neale's framing of why: 'The true validities of the selection methods have not changed over time, but we are now estimating validity more accurately, and more conservatively, than before.' The article also explains that a validity coefficient is a correlation, that 0.00 means no relationship and 1.00 means perfect prediction, and that most selection methods correlate with performance between 0.20 and 0.50.

9054.gloss: A peer-reviewed 2023 journal restating that structured interviews still rank first under the revised estimates while unstructured is significantly lower
9054.verbatim: Samantha Sinclair, 'Applicants' Faith in Recruiters' Intuition Predicts Process Favorability for the Unstructured Employment Interview', Scandinavian Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology, volume 8, issue 1, article 10, DOI 10.16993/sjwop.183, submitted 25 March 2022, accepted 22 June 2023, published 18 September 2023 (study N = 345). The introduction states the position of the field after the revision: unstructured employment interviews often have relatively low interrater reliability (citing Huffcutt et al., 2013), and 'with revised meta-analytic estimates, structured interviews still emerge as the highest ranked selection procedure; while the validity estimate for unstructured interviews is significantly lower (Sackett et al., 2022).' Despite this, the paper notes the unstructured interview has remained the most used method in personnel selection for over a century, and that likely sources of the validity loss in intuitive and holistic approaches include lower consistency and a higher rate of unsystematic errors (Kuncel et al., 2013).

9055.gloss: A recruiting blog that quotes both numbers at once: .51/.38 from Schmidt & Hunter, .42 attributed to Sackett et al. 2023
9055.verbatim: Pin's guide 'Structured Interviews: How to Run Them and Why They Work (2026)' by Jacob Price (published 27 March 2026, updated 26 May 2026) states that according to Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis, unstructured interviews have a predictive validity of .38 and structured interviews .51, describing predictive validity as a measure of how accurately a selection method forecasts job performance, and says the .51 figure improves applicant identification by 34% compared with unstructured conversations. Its summary line reads: 'This format hits .51 validity vs. .38 for unstructured (Schmidt & Hunter), and more recent work by Sackett et al., 2023 puts validity at .42, the top-ranked standalone predictor.' The page also reports the bias effect shrinking from d = .59 in unstructured interviews to d = .23 in structured ones, cites Google's re:Work Structured Interviewing Guide as finding the same pattern across thousands of hires, and notes that only about two-thirds of employers use structured evaluation per Talent Board 2024 CandE research. Its comparison table lists structured interviews as scored on an anchored 1-5 rubric with standardised job-related questions, against subjective impression for unstructured.
